items.title: Identifying generative AI use among genuine responders in online survey research
items.author: Sean B. Cash
items.content: Surveys are compromised not only by bots, but also by the use of AI by genuine human survey respondents. How can researchers ensure that surveys reflect public opinion rather than recycled or programmed content?

items.title: The valence of client and therapist language reflects symptom changes in messaging-based psychotherapy
items.author: Erik C. Nook
items.content: The valence of client and therapist language was associated with changes in clients’ depression and anxiety symptoms across messaging based psychotherapeutic exchanges, showing how affective and linguistic measures can track therapeutic progress.

items.title: Leveraging large language models to map triggers of contamination-related obsessive-compulsive symptoms
items.author: Dirk U. Wulff
items.content: Using LLMs, this study mapped contamination-related obsessive compulsive symptom triggers in 1’495 individuals. Distinct trigger categories across ecological domains and varying intensity were identified, providing a foundation for future translational research.

items.title: Psychological research is increasingly cited in U.S. policy documents especially for education, health and social justice issues
items.author: Jen-Ho Chang
items.content: Using a large-scale dataset linking U.S. policy documents to cited social science papers, this study traces psychology’s policy uptake from 2000–2022 and identifies the paper features, topics, and policy issues most associated with use

items.title: Personality traits are less stable than people think
items.author: Wiebke Bleidorn
items.content: Two studies show that laypeople uniquely rate personality traits as being more stable across the lifespan than 20+ other individual differences, despite the traits having similar and often even larger empirical lifespan changes than those variables

items.title: The role of affective learning biases in daily food behaviour
items.author: Lucas Spierer
items.content: How individuals learn to assign value to cues and actions may help explain how eating behaviours emerge. This study investigated whether reinforcement learning biases are associated with food cravings, consumption, and approach tendencies in daily life.

items.title: Children shift their curiosity from kinds to individuals when items are special or useful
items.author: Kelsey Lucca
items.content: How do children build comprehensive models of the world? Across two experiments with 5- to 9-year-olds in the United States and France, marking items as special or useful shifted children’s curiosity from wanting to learn about kinds to individuals, with select consequences for learning.

items.title: Early parenting is associated with the development of neural reward responsiveness from childhood through adolescence
items.author: Autumn Kujawa
items.content: Reward responsiveness plays an important role in promoting health in youth. We examined neural reward response from childhood through adolescence. Lower positive parenting and higher negative parenting predicted a reduced reward response over time.
